title: Practical Memory Safety
excerpt: Recently: Zig is considering a safe, Fil-C-like compilation target. Fil-C is a “memory safe implementation of C”, and the Zig issue claims this …
content_html:
Recently:

  1. Zig is considering a safe, Fil-C-like compilation target.
  2. Fil-C is a “memory safe implementation of C”, and the Zig issue claims this will be “truly memory safe”.
  3. This is presented as “unlike Rust” because Rust has escape hatches a.k.a. Unsafe Rust.
  4. But it turns out Fil-C’s definition of memory safety is different from Rust’s.
  5. So maybe Fil-C is also unsafe?

You might look at all this and be like, I Ain’t Reading All That. And you might get the vibe that memory safety is something fuzzy and controversial1, with no right or wrong answers… so maybe you should care less about it?

But ’tis not so! Not at all! By the end of this post, I hope to convince you of two seemingly contradictory ideas:

  1. Memory safety can be viewed as a spectrum. We can have more of it - which is good even if the details can be nuanced and frustrating.
  2. There can be a practical definition of memory safety that isn’t about nuance at all - which is also good, especially for you.

So, let’s dig in, starting with the gist of all of this recent hoo-ha ☝️

Unsafe Fil-C

Adapted from this lobste.rs comment, here’s some C code:

struct User {
    char name[8];
    int is_root;
};

struct User* user = malloc(sizeof(struct User));
strcpy(user->name, argv[1]);

This code allocates a User and copies a string from the first command-line argument.

But what happens when the input is 8 characters or longer?

if (user->is_root) {
    printf("I am root!\n");
} else {
    printf("I am not root :(\n");
}

This can print I am root!, even in Fil-C, because strcpy will happily overwrite memory that you own. Fil-C defines memory safety as having having “runtime checks to prevent exploitable memory safety errors”. The above code is not technically “exploitable” so the overwrite is allowed.

This code will trap if you write outside the allocation2, so the proposed Zig mode would totally be safer than Yolo-Zig3, which is a good thing. See also steveklabnik’s comment on HN.

Clearly, if Fil-C makes this code more memory safe, then memory safety as a whole must be a spectrum!

But would you consider this “an exploit”? Would you consider this code “safe”?

These are big questions, and though I love a good technically correct answer, I’d like to contribute a less nuanced answer to the question “what is memory safety” that I think is more practical:

Memory-safe code is code where memory has (1) intuitive and (2) easy to follow rules,
unless there’s a big sign that says otherwise.

In my head, this is also the “non-buoyant water law of memory safety”.

This definition is, obviously, no good for the real experts who design memory models and compilers and CPUs - they’d like to do fun important stuff like proving properties of programs, and eliminating operations that cannot be observed, and so on.

So to be more precise: having a proper technical definition of memory safety is important - insofar as it ensures that safe operations on memory match our general expectations around memory and have rules that can easily be followed correctly.

The unsafe side of the boundary can have complex and even obscure rules,
but if the safe side also has obscure rules that are hard to follow, is it even useful to draw the boundary?

Rules that are simple and enforced automatically are easier to follow correctly than rules that are complex and unchecked.4 However, if there’s an asterisk on each memory access, then what’s the point of the word “safety” anyway?

So, even though Fil-C is safer than Yolo-C and the proposed Memory-Trapping-Zig would be safer than Yolo-Zig, they are not really safe in the only way that matters to you.

They still have unmarked and unchecked memory footguns that you need to check and be constantly aware of, and calling that “memory safe” somewhat belittles the title-case “Memory Safety” that people are raving about (and expecting!).

Conclusion

Memory Safety is great! It works for you: it makes life harder for someone else - the compiler author or the standard library designer - so that you can have a better time working on the things you care about!

There can be some subtlety to the definition, and of course there are also issues unrelated to memory safety that are worth systematically attacking, but the point of having memory safety is to have less subtlety overall.

Or, to borrow Ralf Jung’s phrasing slightly out of context: “When writing safe Rust, you do not have to worry” about the abstract machine. And really, the world provides enough things to worry about without adding that to the list.

Discuss on lobste.rs.

Appendix: Some More Examples

Python CFFI

Python is memory safe: you can use CFFI to do whatever you want:

from cffi import FFI
ffibuilder = FFI()
ffibuilder.cdef("...")

# Or
from ctypes import *
cdll.LoadLibrary("libc.so.6")
libc = CDLL("libc.so.6")

But everything unsafe is literally called C-something. That’s the sign.

Similarly, any language where FFI or unsafe memory access is an explicit construct (unsafe extern "C" in Rust, P/Invoke and unsafe in .Net, or Java’s JNI), can be safe.

Rust /proc/self/mem

A language is not unsafe just because it lets you write to memory like this:

let mut f = fs::OpenOptions::new()
    .write(true)
    .open("/proc/self/mem").unwrap();

Yes, you can do really bad memory crimes with this. However, there’s a clear sign: /proc/self/mem is a great way to say “all bets are off”.

Zig is Unsafe

This is not controversial, but see a previous post.

  1. You might feel that regardless, which is probably more to do with how social media and the internet at large amplify polarization. The good news about our lord and savior Ferris the Crab can sound preachy at times. ↩︎

  2. The allocation is rounded up from 12 to 16 bytes in this case. ↩︎

  3. Fil-C calls classic C “Yolo-C”, and since Zig is adopting these semantics, this seems only fair. ↩︎

  4. It also doesn’t mean that adhering to the rules is easy work - borrow checking can be a fickle goddess 🦀. ↩︎

content_html_zh:
最近：

  1. Zig 正在考虑一个安全的、类似 Fil-C 的编译目标。
  2. Fil-C 是“C 的内存安全实现”，Zig 问题声称这将是“真正的内存安全”。
  3. 这被称为“与 Rust 不同”，因为 Rust 有逃生舱口，又名： 不安全的铁锈。
  4. 但事实证明，Fil-C 对内存安全的定义与 Rust 不同。
  5. 那么也许 Fil-C 也不安全？

你可能会看到这一切，然后说，我没有读完所有这些。 你可能会觉得内存安全是一个模糊且有争议的问题，没有正确或错误的答案…… 所以也许你应该少关心它？

但事实并非如此！ 一点也不！ 在这篇文章的结尾，我希望能让您相信两个看似矛盾的想法：

  1. 内存安全可以被视为一个频谱。 我们可以拥有更多——这很好，即使细节可能微妙且令人沮丧。
  2. 内存安全可以有一个实用的定义，而与细微差别无关——这也很好，尤其是对你来说。

那么，让我们深入探讨，从最近发生的所有事情的要点开始☝️

不安全的 Fil-C

以下是一些 C 代码，改编自 lobste.rs 评论：

struct User {
    char name[8];
    int is_root;
};

struct User* user = malloc(sizeof(struct User));
strcpy(user->name, argv[1]);

此代码分配一个 User 并从第一个命令行参数复制一个字符串。

但是当输入的字符数为 8 个或更长时会发生什么呢？

if (user->is_root) {
    printf("I am root!\n");
} else {
    printf("I am not root :(\n");
}

即使在 Fil-C 中，这也可以打印 I am root!，因为 strcpy 会很乐意覆盖您拥有的内存。 Fil-C 将内存安全定义为具有“运行时检查以防止可利用的内存安全错误”。 从技术上讲，上述代码不可“利用”，因此允许覆盖。

如果您在allocation2之外编写此代码，则会陷入困境，因此建议的 Zig 模式将完全比 Yolo-Zig3 更安全，这是一件好事。 另请参阅 steveklabnik 对 HN 的评论。

显然，如果 Fil-C 使这段代码的内存安全性更高，那么整个内存安全性必定是一个谱系！

但你会认为这是“一种利用”吗？ 您认为这段代码“安全”吗？

这些都是大问题，尽管我喜欢技术上正确的答案，但我想对“什么是内存安全”这个问题提供一个我认为更实用的不太细致的答案：

内存安全代码是指内存具有 (1) 直观性和 (2) 易于遵循规则的代码，除非有一个大标志另有说明。

在我看来，这也是“记忆安全的非浮力水定律”。

显然，这个定义对于设计内存模型、编译器和 CPU 的真正专家来说没有什么好处——他们想做一些有趣的重要事情，比如证明程序的属性，消除无法观察到的操作，等等。

因此，更准确地说：对内存安全有一个正确的技术定义非常重要——因为它可以确保内存上的安全操作符合我们对内存的一般期望，并且具有可以轻松正确遵循的规则。

边界的不安全侧可以有复杂甚至晦涩的规则，但如果安全侧也有难以遵循的晦涩规则，那么划边界还有用吗？

简单且自动执行的规则比复杂且未经检查的规则更容易正确遵循。4 但是，如果每次内存访问都带有星号，那么“安全”一词还有什么意义呢？

因此，尽管 Fil-C 比 Yolo-C 更安全，并且提议的 Memory-Trapping-Zig 也比 Yolo-Zig 更安全，但它们并不是真正安全，因为它们对您来说是唯一重要的方式。

他们仍然拥有未经标记和未经检查的内存枪，您需要检查并不断意识到，并将其称为“内存安全”在某种程度上贬低了人们热衷（并期待！）的标题“内存安全”。

结论

内存安全很棒！ 它对你有用：它会让其他人（编译器作者或标准库设计者）的生活变得更加困难，这样你就可以更好地处理你关心的事情！

这个定义可能有一些微妙之处，当然也有一些与内存安全无关的问题值得系统地解决，但内存安全的要点是总体上不那么微妙。

或者，稍微断章取义地借用 Ralf Jung 的措辞：“在编写安全的 Rust 时，你不必担心”抽象机。 事实上，世界提供了足够多的事情让我们担心，而无需将其添加到列表中。

在 lobste.rs 上讨论。

Python CFFI

Python 是内存安全的：你可以使用 CFFI 做任何你想做的事：

from cffi import FFI
ffibuilder = FFI()
ffibuilder.cdef("...")

# Or
from ctypes import *
cdll.LoadLibrary("libc.so.6")
libc = CDLL("libc.so.6")

但所有不安全的东西都被称为 C-something。 这就是标志。

同样，任何 FFI 或不安全内存访问是显式构造的语言（Rust 中的不安全 extern“C”、P/Invoke 以及 .Net 中的不安全或 Java 的 JNI）都可以是安全的。

生锈 /proc/self/mem

一种语言并不是不安全的，因为它可以让你像这样写入内存：

let mut f = fs::OpenOptions::new()
    .write(true)
    .open("/proc/self/mem").unwrap();

是的，你可以用这个犯下非常糟糕的记忆犯罪。 然而，有一个明显的迹象：/proc/self/mem 是表达“一切皆有可能”的好方法。

Zig 不安全
